hookLine: East and West separate over authority and the Creed; in 1965 pope and patriarch lifted the old excommunications

cards: "That there be no schisms among you." Saint Paul wrote that to a church in Corinth that was splitting into camps: I am of Paul, I am of Apollo. A schism is a tear.
Not a disagreement, which a family can live with, but a tear in the fabric, where people who belong at one table stop sitting at it together. Paul begged that church not to tear.
Long after, a tear came between two churches, East and West. Today, the year that stands for it, and the word for what happened: schism.

teach.b: Two questions had been pulling the Latin West and the Greek East apart. The first was authority: the bishop of Rome's role among all the bishops.
Catholics hold that the pope, as Peter's successor, has a primacy over the whole Church. Orthodox Christians honor Rome's place among the ancient churches but understand that primacy differently.
The second was the Creed. In the West, the line about the Spirit came to read who proceeds from the Father and the Son.

The Catechism says plainly that and the Son was not in the creed confessed at Constantinople, and that the Eastern tradition stresses the Father as the first origin of the Spirit, while the Latin tradition stresses the communion of Father and Son.
Then came the moment the year stands for.

The common declaration Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras made in 1965 recalls it: in 1054, legates of the Roman see pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the Patriarch of Constantinople, Michael Cerularius, and the patriarch and his synod answered with one of their own.
In time it hardened into a lasting break.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
teach.b: In that same declaration, the pope and the patriarch said they regretted the offensive words and gestures on both sides, and they removed the old excommunications from the memory and the midst of the Church.
That didn't end the schism; the two churches are still not in full communion.
But the curses are gone, and the two churches keep talking. A wound, still healing. And under all of it, Jesus's own prayer in John: "That they all may be one."

how: Catholics keep the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity each January, and popes and ecumenical patriarchs have met, prayed together and signed common declarations since the excommunications were lifted.

games.q: you're a pope and a patriarch, meeting long after the old curses. the deep questions aren't solved. what do you do?
o: regret the offensive words on both sides and remove the old excommunications.
renew the curses to keep things clear.
games.why: Paul VI and Athenagoras removed the excommunications from the memory of the Church, without pretending the schism was over.

practice: Bring to mind an Orthodox church you've passed, a Greek or Russian or Romanian or Ukrainian neighbor, or the Orthodox Christians of the world at prayer today, who say the creed of Nicaea and Constantinople and venerate the icons Nicaea defended.
If you pray, pray for them and for the day both churches share one table; if you don't, just wish them well, and stay with that wish.

wordCard.voice: Schism. A tear in the Church's unity, where people who belong at one table stop sharing it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a split or tear; Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 1:10.

carryVoice: Your line: a wound, still healing. Healing this slow is still healing, and it isn't finished yet. See you tomorrow.
